power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: It is relevant to consider that statistical results that cannot reject the null hypotheses within the Null Hypothesis Significance Testing approach (the most common approach in the studies examined above), are not outright support of the null hypotheses. Instead, the correct reading is that the alternative hypotheses were not supported on those occasions. That is, the phenomena under investigation are not proved to be nonexistent: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Very often, authors interested in ESP and PK ignore or do not take into account the fact that expected effects are often small, as documented in the available meta-analyses (e.g., Storm & Tressoldi, 2023; see also Cardeña, 2018). For example, the expected effect sizes in tasks requiring a forced-choice in a normal state of consciousness range from .009 to .02 (Storm & Tressoldi, 2023; see also Cardeña, 2018). To achieve a statistical power of a minimum .80, and the expected effect size set to .05 above the expected chance of .5, with a one-tailed binomial test, requires 620 trials (or 620 participants performing a single trial).

text.text: This review systematically investigated preregistered studies concerning extra-sensory perception (ESP) and mind-matter interaction (micropsychokinesis; i.e., micro-PK), available up to October 2026.
The primary aims were to evaluate their outcomes and compare the percentage of positive findings with those observed in mainstream psychology.
Our methodology adhered to the PRISMA Guidelines.
We searched major preregistration repositories, including the Open Science Framework and the Koestler Parapsychology Unit (KPU) Study Registry, and relevant meta-analyses.
Inclusion criteria focused on completed studies with available preregistration and final results only for confirmatory hypotheses.
A positive outcome was defined as the support of at least one confirmatory hypothesis, strictly following preregistered procedures and statistics without deviation.
A total of 50 studies with a total of 60 experiments, met the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Of these, 17 experiments (28.3%) reported a positive outcome, and 20 confirmatory hypotheses out of 97 (20.6%) were positive.

Interestingly, and contrary to some expectations, a broader comparison indicated that preregistered studies concerning ESP and PK did not necessarily exhibit a much lower proportion of confirmed hypotheses when compared with results for preregistered studies in mainstream psychology.

Most disciplines, including psychology and the sub-discipline of parapsychology, recognize the concerns in recent years over research credibility and reproducibility (Bošnjak et al., 2021; Logg & Dorison, 2021; Sasaki & Yamada, 2020; Waldron & Allen, 2022).

text.text: Consequently, there is an increased focus on preregistration as a means by which questionable research practices (QRPs) can be addressed.

These QRPs include p-hacking (e.g., preferencing some p values over others), HARKing (hypothesizing after the results are known and presenting them as if they were pre-planned rather than post hoc), and selective reporting (Krypotos et al., 2022; Nosek et al., 2019; Sasaki & Yamada, 2020; Simmons et al., 2021; van den Akker et al., 2024).

text.text: In summary, preregistration is a major contributor to transparency in research, and research designs are greatly improved in terms of statistical power and sample size.

Also, increased reliability of statistical findings builds confidence, especially when biases like p-hacking and HARKing are eliminated, provided of course preregistration rules are followed and researchers adhere to the registered plan.

Preregistration also plays a crucial role in enhancing the credibility and trustworthiness of research dealing with controversial phenomena like extra-sensory perception (ESP) or mind-matter interaction (i.e., psychokinesis; PK), where findings often face heightened skepticism and challenges to reproducibility (Kekecs et al., 2023).

text.text: All studies, according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, were analyzed by the first author (P.T.), who also conducted the statistical tests on the study data (L.S. checked the database and statistics).
Fifty studies met the inclusion and exclusion criteria: 38 studies (76%) of these were peer-reviewed, see (x) above.

In terms of number of the studies with one (or more) legitimate confirmed hypothesis, see (viii) above, there are more confirmatory hypotheses than studies: 97 confirmatory hypotheses, and 60 experiments.

In terms of 'outcomes', see (ix) above, only 20 confirmatory hypotheses out of 97 (20.6%) were 'positive, which is to say true to the preregistered wording (i.e., they followed the exact preregistered procedure and statistics, and did not deviate from it).
If our count is based on experiments alone, 17 out of 60 (28.3%) were 'positive'.

A post-hoc observation, evidenced that the series of ten experiments related to the unconscious influence on the randomness of random number generators, carried out by Markus Maier and collaborators, resulted in 90% of failed confirmatory outcomes.
Filtering out these experiments, the percentage of positive outcomes raised to 34%.

The most investigated task (psi modality)-see (iii) above-was Precognition (including Precall, Retropriming, Retroactive Facilitation, and I Ching) with 22 of 60 experiments (36.6%), PK with 19 experiments (31.6%), Presentiment with 7 studies (11.6%), Clairvoyance (including Remote Viewing and Subtle Energy Detection) with 4 studies (6.6%), and Telepathy with 5 studies (8.3%).

One unique study that tested Morphic Resonance (Vernon et al, 2021) was excluded from categorization (due to the difficulty of slotting it into a recognized category), but another tested Remote Viewing and PK (Mossbridge et al., 2024), so the final total of studies for this exercise was still 60.

A participant is usually designated 'selected' because they were intentionally recruited for possessing characteristics experimenters deem psi-conducive.

Such participants often claim prior psi experience, or they practice a mental discipline (e.g., meditation, yoga, energy healing), or they are creative and/or open to new experiences, or they have strong emotional sensitivity or intuitive tendencies.

There were 7 experiments out of 17 (41.1%) with at least one statistically supported hypothesis with selected participants, whereas there were 10 experiments out of 17 (58.8%) with at least one statistically supported hypothesis with unselected participants.

The present systematic review aimed to critically evaluate the outcomes of preregistered studies investigating ESP and PK, and to compare their rate of positive outcomes against those observed in mainstream psychology.

This inquiry is particularly pertinent given the broader scientific community's increasing emphasis on research credibility and reproducibility, with preregistration serving as a key strategy to mitigate QRPs such as p-hacking, HARKing, and selective reporting.
Our review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA Guidelines, systematically identified and analyzed 50 preregistered ESP and PK studies.

Each study was rigorously assessed for variables including its results source, preregistration repository, task type, consciousness state, response format, participant selection, number of confirmatory hypotheses, confirmed hypotheses, overall outcome (positive or negative), and peer-review status.

A positive outcome was specifically defined as the successful support of at least one confirmatory hypothesis, adhering strictly to the preregistered procedures and statistical analyses without deviations.

Our search encompassed major preregistration repositories like the Open Science Framework and the KPU Study Registry, alongside relevant metaanalyses, ensuring comprehensive coverage of completed studies with available documentation for both preregistration and final results.
The findings indicate that 17 out of 60 experiments (28.3%) reported positive outcomes.
On confirmatory hypotheses only, there are 20 out of 97 (20.6%) that were statistically supported (confirmed).
We compared the above results with the positive outcome rates that can be found in mainstream preregistered psychological studies, as illustrated in Figure 1.

text.text: Interestingly, and contrary to some expectations regarding the impact of preregistration, this review found that preregistered studies did not necessarily exhibit a much lower proportion of positive results when compared to mainstream studies.
This is to say, there is a common belief that preregistration leads to fewer positive findings, because it reduces QRPs like p-hacking or HARKing.
This belief is supported by historical analyses. Wiseman et al. (2019) compared Registered Reports (RRs) against non-RRs published in the European Journal of Parapsychology between 1976 and 1993.
text.formatted: This belief is supported by historical analyses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Wiseman et al. (2019)</ref> compared Registered Reports (RRs) against non-RRs published in the European Journal of Parapsychology between 1976 and 1993.

text.text: They found that only 8.4% of hypotheses in RRs were statistically significant, compared to 28.4% in non-RRs, suggesting that the introduction of registration effectively reduced false positives driven by QRPs during that era.
However, the current landscape appears different.
Our review found that preregistration in contemporary studies did not see psi effects diminish to the same extent.
This finding suggests that modern preregistration may not necessarily suppress positive outcomes as much as some critics or skeptics have assumed based on earlier implementation models.
Parapsychologists can design effective studies under strict preregistration controls.
We also checked on psi modalities, altered states of consciousness, and experimental designs.
Precognition was the most common modality tested (36.6%).
Participants were more commonly tested in normal (waking) states (76.6%), and the most common design was Forced-Choice (63.3%).
Finally, unselected participants were tested almost twice as often as selected participants (71.7% vs.
28.3%, respectively), but there appeared to be no performance advantage in the latter group.
One limitation of this study is that at present there are no independent criteria to assess the quality of preregistrations.
One solution is to preregister the study as a registered report (https://www.cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports), where in stage 1, the preregistration is peer reviewed.
text.formatted: One solution is to preregister the study as a registered report (<ref type="url" target="https://www.cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports">https://www.cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports</ref>), where in stage 1, the preregistration is peer reviewed.

text.text: Even if all preregistrations submitted to the KPU Registry are reviewed by Caroline Watt and Jim Kennedy, allowing the authors to have feedback about the clarity and the details of their study, there is no control of the adherence between what was preregistered and what is reported in the final reports or the published peer-reviewed papers.
Comparing preregistrations with final reports is difficult.
It requires considerable time, careful checking, and expertise, and judgements.
Checking the quality of preregistered methods is also difficult.
It requires expertise, close attention to detail in particular in the definition on how the confirmatory hypotheses will be tested, with particular attention to the statistical power.

In conclusion, while preregistration significantly contributes to enhancing the transparency and methodological rigor of research in controversial areas like ESP and PK, its impact on the rate of positive findings or the direct prevention of specific biases like p-hacking and HARKing may be more nuanced than often assumed.
The positive outcome rate observed in this systematic review provides valuable empirical data for ongoing discussions about research integrity and reproducibility within parapsychological studies.

It is relevant to consider that statistical results that cannot reject the null hypotheses within the Null Hypothesis Significance Testing approach (the most common approach in the studies examined above), are not outright support of the null hypotheses.
Instead, the correct reading is that the alternative hypotheses were not supported on those occasions.
That is, the phenomena under investigation are not proved to be nonexistent: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Very often, authors interested in ESP and PK ignore or do not take into account the fact that expected effects are often small, as documented in the available meta-analyses (e.g., Storm & Tressoldi, 2023; see also Cardeña, 2018).
